newsitem.title: UK: S&P assigns Russia BB minus long-term, B short-term.
newsitem.headline: S&P assigns Russia BB minus long-term, B short-term.

text.p: Standard & Poor's on Monday assigned Russia a long-term sovereign rating of BB minus and a short-term B for the country's foreign currency debt, an S&P official said.
S&P, which also said the outlook on the long-term rating was stable, said in a statement that key factors constraining the rating were --
-- the government's short economic management track record and, especially, the political and administrative difficulties it faces raising tax revenues,
-- the challenge of leadership in a country with a still developing democrating culture and political institutions,
-- and a weak legal system, including lax enforcement that continues to foster widespread corruption, discourages foreign investment, and acts as a drag on overall economic activity.

"To date, Russia's fiscal consolidation has relied heavily on sequestering cash expenditures, a costly practice and one difficult to sustain in the face of persistent public sector wage arrears, as well as unmet social spending needs."

S&P also said, "President Yeltsin's current illness highlights the risk that changes at the top may, at least for a time, halt the reform process and undermine the authorities' ability to pursue prudent and consistent economic policies."
The agency said elements supporting the rating included --
-- the government's and central bank's heightened commitment to an orthodox economic programme since 1994, particularly with respect to disinflation,
-- general government debt, estimated at 47 percent of GDP this year, in line with that of similarly rated sovereigns,
-- a manageable external debt service profile,
-- contingent liabilities broadly in line with those of similarly rated sovereigns,
-- and strong international backing for Russia's transformation to a market-based economy that should continue medium term.

S&P said in regard to the ratings outlook, progress in implementing key reforms may stall if Yeltsin left office prematurely. "Still, in that event, current policies probably will not be completely reversed," it said.

"Rapid privatisation has crteated a new class of property owners with a strong vested interest in the reform process, while the rapid decline in inflation has strengthened popular and parliamentary support for orthodox economic policies."
It also said that with output poised to begin growing next year, the current account is likely to shift from a surplus of one percent of GDP in 1996 to deficits in the medium term.

"However, the public external debt burden could fall further assuming the fiscal deficit can be contained. Russia's manageable external debt service, along with continued official external financial support, consequently should cushion its credit standing against most economic and political shocks," S&P said.
